Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Meet the Poem — Read Aloud and First Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Recite (p.1): teacher-led read-aloud of the full poem with illustrations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or draws attention to the illustrations on p.1 — a man searching in pockets, under a chair, near a window — and asks students to guess what the poem might be about. This picture walk primes observation before any words are read.

Teacher reads the full poem aloud at a natural pace, pointing to each stanza as it is read. Students follow along in their textbooks, listening for the repeated phrases ‘He can’t…’ and ‘He checked… He glanced… He searched…’.

Teacher reads the poem a second time with deliberate expression and invites the class to join in chorally on the repeated lines. Students echo-read each ‘He can’t…’ and ‘He checked…’ line immediately after the teacher models it.

Students read the poem aloud once more in two groups — one group reads the narrator’s lines and the other reads the ‘He…’ action lines. Teacher guides pacing and expression, drawing attention to the bouncy four-beat rhythm.
Teacher asks two or three students to say in one sentence what happens in the poem. No written response yet — this is a quick oral check of first understanding before the close of the sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s humour rests on the irony of searching for something in plain sight; let students discover the punchline at the final stanza without revealing it earlier. Anaphora — the repeated ‘He can’t…’ — is the poem’s key structural device and choral reading makes it audible; stress these lines in your model read. Avoid rushing the picture walk on p.1, as the five illustrations sequence the search visually and support comprehension before reading begins.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion — Answering Questions on the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.2): discuss and answer three comprehension questions on the poem.

time_bands.activity: Students chant the poem together from their textbooks as a quick warm-up. Teacher listens for the anaphoric ‘He can’t…’ lines and encourages expressive stress on those phrases.

Teacher poses question 1 — ‘What is Papa searching for?’ — aloud to the class. Students locate the answer in the first stanza, share their responses orally, and then write one sentence in their notebooks.

Teacher poses question 2 — ‘What are the possible places where Papa can find it?’ — and reads the third stanza together with the class. Students list the places mentioned (pockets, under the chair, near the window) in their notebooks and discuss whether these are all the places the poem mentions.

Teacher poses question 3 — ‘At last, where does Papa find his lost item?’ — and students read the final stanza aloud. Students write the answer in one sentence, and two or three volunteers share their sentences with the class for quick peer feedback.

Teacher draws attention to the comic irony — the spectacles were on Papa’s head all along — and invites a brief show of hands: has anyone ever searched for something that was already with them? This oral moment closes the comprehension work on the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together, students will have the repeated search lines fresh in mind; use that familiarity to anchor question 2 by pointing to the stanza ‘He checked inside his pockets…’ on p.1. A common difficulty at this level is locating textual evidence rather than guessing; prompt students to point to the line before writing their answer. Question 3’s answer — spectacles are on Papa’s head — is in the final stanza, and students who miss the humour may answer ‘on his chair’; direct them to re-read the last four lines.

periods.activity_title: Think, Discuss and Share — Experiences of Losing Things

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (pp.2–3): guided discussion on chores Papa can’t do, gratitude, and misplaced things at home and school.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the first discussion prompt: ‘Apart from reading, what other chores might Papa find difficult without his spectacles?’ Students brainstorm in pairs for a brief exchange, then share ideas with the class. Teacher lists a few student suggestions on the board.

Teacher poses the second prompt: ‘What makes your papa or a family elder happy?’ Students take turns sharing one idea each in a brief round. Teacher models one example to reduce hesitation and keeps responses moving briskly around the room.

Students draw a simple two-column table in their notebooks — one for things misplaced at home and who helps find them, and a second for school. Teacher guides the class to fill in two or three rows together as a shared example before students complete the rest independently and then read their entries aloud to a partner.

Teacher brings the class together: ‘How do you say thank you to the person who helps you find something?’ Students share phrases of gratitude aloud; teacher writes two or three on the board and the class practises saying them expressively to a partner.

Teacher closes the discussion by connecting back to the poem: the child in the poem helps Papa just as the people students named help them. One student is invited to say one sentence about a time they helped someone find a lost object.

periods.teacher_notes: The discussion about what Papa cannot do without spectacles (cooking, driving, recognising faces) expands vocabulary naturally; accept all reasonable suggestions and note vivid verbs students use. The misplaced-things tables are meant to be personal and spoken, not just written; circulate while students write and prompt quiet students with a question about their bag or desk. Gratitude expressions are the communicative heart of this task — model a warm, genuine tone so students move beyond a routine ‘thank you’.

periods.activity_title: Words for Father and Sound Discrimination — Listening Activity

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.2): share words for ‘father’ in different languages and list them.
Let us Listen (p.8): listen to word pairs and encircle those that sound different.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the word ‘Papa’ from the poem’s title and asks: ‘What word do you use at home for your father?’ Students call out words in their own languages; teacher writes them on the board. Students copy the class list into their notebooks and each reads one word aloud clearly.
Teacher explains that English borrows and shares words with many languages, and ‘Papa’ is one such shared word. Students say the word in a quick choral voice to celebrate this multilingual moment.

Teacher introduces the listening task from p.8: ‘I will read word pairs aloud. Listen carefully — if the two words sound the same, do nothing; if they sound different, encircle the pair in your book.’ Teacher reads each pair three to four times at a steady pace, pausing between pairs.

Teacher continues reading the remaining word pairs at the same pace, repeating each pair three to four times. After all pairs are read, teacher reads each pair once more while students check their choices, then two or three students share their answers orally for a quick class confirmation.

Teacher selects two or three contrasting pairs — for example, ‘sun–son’ (same) and ‘bed–bad’ (different) — and asks students to explain why one pair sounds the same and the other does not, reinforcing vowel-sound awareness.

periods.teacher_notes: The ‘words for father’ activity celebrates linguistic diversity; note all student contributions warmly and avoid correcting pronunciation of home-language words. For the listening task on p.8, pairs such as ‘sun–son’ and ‘knot–not’ are homophones and should NOT be encircled; pairs like ‘bed–bad’ and ‘fair–fear’ sound different and should be encircled — confirm this distinction clearly before the task begins. Read each pair with natural speed and equal stress on both words so students are not misled by your intonation.

periods.activity_title: Word Work — Ordering, Pairs and Spelling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.3): arrange word groups in ascending order by size or weight.
Let us Learn B (p.4): fill in ‘a pair of…’ phrases using pictures of paired objects.
Let us Learn C (p.5): encircle the correctly spelt word in each set of three.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models task A on p.3 using the first group aloud: ‘Handkerchief — the smallest; then Towel; then Sari; then Bedsheet — the largest.’ Students complete the remaining four groups independently, then write two original examples following the same size-or-weight pattern.

Teacher holds up the textbook open to p.4 and asks: ‘What object do you see in picture 1?’ Students identify each object and complete the seven ‘a pair of…’ phrases. Teacher checks responses orally by pointing to each picture and asking a student to complete the phrase aloud.

Teacher writes one incorrect spelling on the board — for example ‘baloon’ — and asks students to spot what is wrong before turning to p.5. Students work through all ten spelling items independently, circling their choice, and then the class reads each correct spelling aloud together as teacher confirms.

Teacher asks: ‘Which word in task C also appears in our poem?’ Students locate ‘spectacles’ in both the poem and the spelling list, connecting the word across the two activities as a closing observation.

periods.teacher_notes: Task A is a conceptual sequencing exercise, not alphabetical ordering; clarify that students are ordering by physical size or weight and give a concrete example such as a pen versus a ruler versus a table before they begin. The word ‘pair’ in task B links directly to the poem’s title — Papa lost ‘his only pair’; highlight this connection so the vocabulary lands in context. In task C, ‘receive’ trips many students because of the i-before-e pattern; give it a moment of explicit attention after students have attempted it.

periods.activity_title: Prepositions in Context and Poem-to-Story Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn D (p.6): complete a story using correct prepositions from the word bank.
Let us Write (pp.7–8): retell the poem as a short story; share with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story cloze on p.6 aloud, pausing at each blank. Students suggest which preposition from the word bank fits, and teacher writes their suggestions on the board before confirming. Students then write the completed paragraph in their notebooks.

Teacher models the writing task aloud: ‘Today, my father is unhappy. He has lost his spectacles — his only pair. He cannot read the newspaper or watch TV.’ Teacher writes these two or three sentences on the board, thinking aloud about which details from the poem to include and which order to tell them in.

Students write their own story version of the poem in their notebooks, following the starter ‘Today, my father is unhappy…’ and working through the events: searching in pockets, under the chair, near the window, and then the cheerful discovery that the spectacles were on his head. Teacher circulates, prompts students who are stuck, and encourages them to use the poem’s language naturally.

Two or three students read their stories aloud to the class. After each, teacher invites one peer comment: ‘What detail did you enjoy?’ This oral sharing gives writers an immediate audience and closes the writing task within the sitting.

Teacher draws the two tasks together: the prepositions in task D describe where Papa looked, and the story retells that search. Students name one preposition from task D that they used in their story, making the grammar-in-context connection explicit.

periods.teacher_notes: Task D’s prepositions — around, after, before, in, above, on, among — describe spatial and temporal relationships; the story cloze grounds them in a searching narrative that echoes the poem, so students should have natural intuitions about most blanks. In the writing task, students sometimes summarise the poem in one sentence rather than narrating it as a story; model the difference between ‘Papa lost his spectacles’ (summary) and ‘Papa began searching everywhere’ (narrative) before students write. Keep the sharing brief and warm — the goal is a real audience, not a performance.

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text — Puzzles, Optical Illusions and a Riddle

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do A (p.9): move 3 matchsticks to form 3 squares from a 4-square arrangement.
Let us Do B (p.9): optical illusion — focus on the red star, then shift gaze to the candle.
Let us Do C (p.10): find the hidden ‘d’ in the grid of ‘b’ letters.
Just for Fun (p.10): solve the riddle — what goes to market, comes home, and cries?

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens to p.9 and introduces the matchstick puzzle in task A. Students try to solve it individually first, then discuss with a neighbour; teacher invites a volunteer to explain their solution. Emphasis is on reasoning aloud — how did you decide which matchsticks to move?

Teacher introduces the optical illusion in task B, guiding students through the steps: look at the candle illustration on p.9, then bring the red star close to the nose and shift focus. Students try in pairs and describe what they observe. Teacher connects this to the poem’s theme of seeing — or not seeing — what is right in front of you.

Students open to p.10 and hunt for the hidden ‘d’ in the grid of ‘b’ letters in task C. The first student to find it raises a hand silently; teacher confirms. The class discusses how easily the eye can miss a small difference — a neat parallel to Papa’s own oversight.

Teacher reads the riddle on p.10 aloud — ‘I go to the market, I lovingly bring you home, I sit in front of you, and I cry, cry, cry. What is it?’ — and gives students time to think. Students share their guesses orally, explain their reasoning, and then the answer (an onion) is revealed and discussed.
Teacher invites students to recite the poem one final time from memory or from the book, ending the chapter’s work on a celebratory, expressive note. One student is invited to perform with gestures.

periods.teacher_notes: The matchstick task and the letter grid both reward sustained visual attention — the same quality the poem gently teases Papa for lacking. If physical matchsticks are available, allow pairs to manipulate them; if not, students can sketch on paper. The riddle’s answer — an onion — surprises most students; give enough silence after reading it for genuine thinking before accepting guesses. The closing recitation is optional but ties the chapter’s oral work together warmly.

items.source_lo: Student reads with expression and retrieves information using a humorous narrative poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Humorous poem about Papa searching for spectacles found on his own head.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 1 beginning “He checked inside his pockets.” Which of the following best describes what Papa does in those lines?

options.label: A
options.text: Papa asks the child to search the house for him.

options.label: B
options.text: Papa decides to buy a new pair of spectacles.

options.label: C
options.text: Papa finds his spectacles inside his coat pocket.

options.label: D
options.text: Papa looks in his pockets, under his chair, and near the window.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have missed that Papa searches alone; no one is asked to help until the child speaks in the final stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student likely confused the places searched with the actual location of the spectacles.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have recalled the story cloze on p.6 rather than the poem itself.

items.source_lo: Student reads with expression and retrieves information using a humorous narrative poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Humorous poem about Papa searching for spectacles found on his own head.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the child tells Papa to stop and then goes up close. What does the child discover, and why is this moment funny? Write two to three sentences using details from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The child discovers that Papa’s spectacles are right there on his head, not lost at all. This is funny because Papa searched everywhere — in his pockets, under the chair, near the window — without realising the spectacles were with him all along.

items.source_lo: Student discusses personal experiences and discriminates between similar sounds using a poem and listening exercise as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Guided discussion on Papa’s chores, gratitude, misplaced things; listening to homophone and near-homophone word pairs.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read two word pairs aloud. Listen carefully and say whether the words in each pair sound the same or different.

options.text: The words ‘bed’ and ‘bad’ sound the same.
The words ‘fair’ and ‘fear’ sound the same.
The words ‘heal’ and ‘heel’ sound the same.
The words ‘sun’ and ‘son’ sound the same.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True (sun and son are homophones; they sound the same). 2 — False (bed and bad have different vowel sounds; they sound different). 3 — True (heal and heel are homophones; they sound the same). 4 — False (fair has the ‘air’ sound and fear has the ‘ear’ sound; they sound different).

items.item_stem: Think about something you often misplace at home or at school. Tell the class: what is the object, who helps you find it, and how do you thank that person? Speak in three or four sentences.

expected_elements: Names a specific object they misplace.
Identifies a person who helps find it.

items.source_lo: Student retells a poem as a short narrative prose piece using a comic poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Retelling ‘Papa’s Spectacles’ as a prose story beginning ‘Today, my father is unhappy…’.
items.item_stem: Read the caption and choose the best answer. A story retelling of ‘Papa’s Spectacles’ should include which of the following details?

options.label: A
options.text: Papa borrows a neighbour’s spectacles and reads the newspaper happily.

options.label: B
options.text: Papa decides he does not need spectacles because the child reads for him.

options.label: C
options.text: Papa searches his pockets, the chair, and the window before the child finds the spectacles on his head.

options.label: D
options.text: The child loses her own spectacles and Papa helps her search for them.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has invented an ending not in the poem; they may not have read the final stanza carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has reversed the roles of the child and Papa in the poem.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has invented a resolution that does not appear anywhere in the poem.

items.item_stem: Write a short story retelling the events of the poem ‘Papa’s Spectacles’ in your own words. Begin with: ‘Today, my father is unhappy…’ and include at least three things Papa tried to do or places he searched. End with the cheerful discovery.

expected_elements: Mentions Papa unable to do at least one daily task.
Names at least three places Papa searched.
Ends with child’s discovery — spectacles on Papa’s head.
